Friendship shapes children’s predictions of emotion responses following conflicting outcomes

2026-10-15

runsheet = runsheet %>% 
  filter(!sub.num %in% exclusions$sub.num)

  select(sub.num, age.months, age.years, sex, story.order, exclude.story, exclude.story.reason, story,

Data Cleaning and Wrangling

Emotion Predictions

#Matching story information 
data = merge(data, story.info, by = c("story.order", "story"))

data = data%>%
  arrange(sub.num, trial)


# Recode Emotions & EToMs
data = data %>% 
  mutate(happy = case_when(happy == "Very happy" ~ 3,
                           happy == "Happy" ~ 2, 
                           happy == "A little happy" ~ 1,
                           happy == "Not happy at all" ~0),
         sad = case_when(sad == "Very sad" ~ -3,
                         sad == "Sad" ~ -2,
                         sad == "A little sad" ~ -1,
                         sad == "Not sad at all" ~ 0)) %>%
  mutate(emotion.score = happy + sad, .after = sad) %>%
  filter(is.na(exclude.story) | exclude.story != "Y") %>%
  mutate(etoms.empathy = etoms.empathy/5,
         etoms.nice.tom = etoms.nice.tom/5,
         etoms.nasty.tom = etoms.nasty.tom/6) %>%
  drop_na(emotion.score)

#For models - Effect coding
model.data = data%>%
  mutate(relationship.type = ifelse(relationship.type == "friends", 1, -1),
         context.type = ifelse(context.type == "competition", 1, -1),
         outcome.type = ifelse(outcome.type == "positive", 1, -1),
         character.gender = ifelse(character.gender == "girl", 1, -1),
         first.relationship = ifelse(first.relationship == "friends", 1, -1), 
         first.context = ifelse(first.context == "competition", 1, -1), 
         first.outcome = ifelse(first.outcome == "positive", 1, -1),
         age.years = age.years - mean(age.years, na.rm = T),
         etoms.empathy = etoms.empathy - mean(etoms.empathy, na.rm = T),
         etoms.nice.tom = etoms.nice.tom - mean(etoms.nice.tom, na.rm = T),
         etoms.nasty.tom = etoms.nasty.tom - mean(etoms.nasty.tom, na.rm = T),
         exploratory.mixed.emotion = ifelse(exploratory.mixed.emotion == "yes", 1, 0),
         sub.num = as.factor(sub.num))

Explanations

exp.wrangle = data %>% 
  dplyr::select(sub.num, story.order) %>% 
  group_by(sub.num) %>%
  slice_head(n=1) %>%
  ungroup() 

explanations = merge(explanations, exp.wrangle, by = c("sub.num"))
explanations = merge(explanations, story.info, by = c("story.order", "story", "trial"), all.x = TRUE) %>% 
  rename(Category = code,
         Response = response) %>%
  drop_na(Category)

explanations = explanations %>%
  mutate(emotion.congruence = case_when(outcome.type == "positive" & explanation == "happy.explanation" ~ "Congruent Outcome x Emotion",
                                        outcome.type == "negative" & explanation == "sad.explanation" ~ "Congruent Outcome x Emotion",
                                        outcome.type == "positive" & explanation == "sad.explanation" ~ "Incongruent Outcome x Emotion",
                                        outcome.type == "negative" & explanation == "happy.explanation" ~ "Incongruent Outcome x Emotion",
                                        TRUE ~ NA)) %>%
  mutate(CategoryHierarchy = case_when(Category %in% c("own.outcome", "other.outcome") ~ "Outcome Information",
                                       Category %in% c("relationship", "other.directed.concern") ~ "Social Information",
                                       Category %in% c("mixed.reasoning") ~ "Intergrated Reasoning",
                                       Category %in% c("mitigation.reappraisal", "desire.value") ~ "Other Explanatory Reasoning",
                                       Category %in% c("other") ~ "Uninformative",
                                       TRUE ~ NA)) %>%
  mutate(Category = case_when(Category == "own.outcome" ~ "Own Outcome",
                              Category == "other.outcome" ~ "Other Outcome",
                              Category == "relationship" ~ "Relationship",
                              Category == "other.directed.concern" ~ "Other-Directed Concern",
                              Category == "mixed.reasoning" ~ "Integrated Reasoning",
                              Category == "mitigation.reappraisal" ~ "Mitigation or Reappraisal",
                              Category == "desire.value" ~ "Desire or Value",
                              Category == "other" ~ "Other",
                              TRUE ~ NA)) %>%
  mutate(SociallyRelevantResponse = ifelse(Category %in% c("Other Outcome", "Other-Directed Concern", "Relationship", "Integrated Reasoning"), 
                                           1,
                                           0)) %>%
  drop_na(Response, Category)

Emotion Predictions

To test our hypothesis that children’s emotion ratings will vary by relationship and outcome type, we will conduct a mixed-effect linear regression on children’s mixed-emotion score across all stories. Relationship type (friends vs. rivals), outcome type (positive vs. negative), participant age in months, and their interactions will be included as fixed effects, and participant number will be included as a random effect. Fixed effects will be dummy-coded and mean-centered. The contribution of each factor to explaining variance in children’s judgments will be determined via nested model comparisons between the full model and a reduced model without the factor under consideration. If the full model incurs a converging error (i.e., the variance of participant as a random effect is too low), we will remove participant as a random effect from all models for this analysis.

Full model: emotion score ~ relationship type * outcome type * age + (1 | sub.num)

A 2-way interaction between relationship type and outcome type, or a 3-way interaction between relationship type, outcome type, and age, will be taken as support for this hypothesis.

We may also observe a main effect of outcome type, where negative outcome stories have more negative emotion scores and positive outcome stories have more positive emotion scores, but the strength of this effect should change across relationship types and/or relationship type and age (i.e., the 2- or 3-way interactions).

We will run planned comparisons of mixed-emotion scores across the four stories. The following pairwise comparisons will be conducted with Bonferroni corrections: friends positive vs. friends negative rivals positive vs. rivals negative friends positive vs. rivals positive friends negative vs. rivals negative

We expect a significant difference in the comparisons between rivals positive vs. rivals negative. However, we should only observe significant differences in the other comparisons if children’s emotion scores are influenced by relationship type. We will also be conducting bayesian analyses to provide additional support for any null comparisons.

Descriptives

data %>%
  group_by(outcome.type, relationship.type) %>%
  select(outcome.type, relationship.type, emotion.score) %>%
  get_summary_stats(type = "mean_sd") %>%
  dplyr::select(-c(variable))

Full Model

emotion.mod0 = lmer(emotion.score ~ relationship.type * outcome.type * age.years + (1 | sub.num), 
                    data = model.data,
                    control = lmerControl(check.conv.singular = .makeCC(action = "ignore", tol = 1e-4)))

drop1(emotion.mod0, test = "Chisq", ddf = "lme4", scope = . ~ .,)

Planned Comparisons

Why Explanations

Children’s why explanations will be transcribed and coded into one of the following categories:

Own Outcome: References what happened to the target: success/failure, winning/losing, or receiving/not receiving the desired resource Other Outcome: References what happened to the other character. Relationship: Invokes the friendship, dislike, or other relationship between the characters as relevant to the emotion. Other-Directed Concern: Explains the target’s emotion in terms of caring about, feeling for, or emotionally responding to the other character’s outcome or welfare. Mixed Reasoning: Integrates both outcome and relationship to explain the target’s emotional response. Desire or Value: Explains emotion in terms of how much the target wants, likes, or values the outcome/resource. Mitigation or Reappraisal: Reduces, reframes, compensates for, or proposes a way to repair the emotional significance of an outcome. Other: Does not provide an interpretable explanation for the predicted emotion.

Descriptives

  group_by(sub.num) %>%
  slice_head(n=1) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(testing.location = ifelse(sub.num < 115, "Museum", "Online")) %>%
  group_by(testing.location) %>%
  summarise(n = length(testing.location)) %>%
  mutate(percent = n/sum(n)*100)
explanations %>%
  filter(Category != "NA") %>%
  group_by(Category) %>%
  summarise(n = length(Category)) %>%
  mutate(percent = round(n/sum(n)*100,digits = 1)) %>%
  arrange(-percent)

Analysis

We fit a mixed-effects logistic regression predicting whether an explanation references socially relevant information from relationship type, emotion congruence, and their interaction, with participant as a random intercept.

explanations.mod = explanations %>% mutate(relationship.type = ifelse(relationship.type == "friends", 1, -1),
                        emotion.congruence = ifelse(emotion.congruence == "Congruent Outcome x Emotion", 1, -1))

explanations.mod0 = glmer(SociallyRelevantResponse ~ relationship.type * emotion.congruence + (1 | sub.num),
                          family = binomial(link = "logit"),
      data = explanations.mod)
drop1(explanations.mod0, test = "Chisq", ddf = "lme4", scope = . ~ .,)

Supplementary Analyses

Empathy and Theory of Mind Scale

There may be individual differences in children’s sensitivity to others’ outcomes, regardless of the relationship type or outcome. As an exploratory analysis, caregivers will be asked to complete the Empathy and Theory of Mind Scale (EToMS, Wang & Wang, 2015). We’ll calculate mean scores based on caregivers’ responses to the three subscales: empathy, nice ToM, and nasty ToM. To determine whether children’s caregiver-reported empathy or ToM predicts their mixed-emotion scores, we will conduct three additional analyses by adding their subscale score as a fixed effect and its interaction with relationship type and outcome type.

emotion score ~ relationship type * outcome type * age + etoms + etoms:relationship type:outcome type + (1 | sub.num)

It’s possible that children with greater empathy will be more likely to report emotion ratings reflective of mixed emotions, regardless of the relationship or outcome. However, it’s also possible that children’s ability to engage in perspective taking and general ToM will be related to their responses.

emtrends(emotion.mod3, ~ outcome.type | relationship.type, var = "etoms.nasty.tom") %>% pairs(infer = c(TRUE, TRUE), adjust = "Bonferroni")

Context Type

Half of the stories participants heard were about physical rewards, while the other half were about competitive scenarios. To determine whether one context had greater influence on children’s emotion scores, we will conduct our confirmatory analysis again, including context type and its 2-, 3-, and 4-way interactions in the full model as dummy-coded, mean-centered fixed effects.

emotion.mod4 = lmer(emotion.score ~ relationship.type * outcome.type * context.type + (1|sub.num), 
                    data = model.data,
                    control = lmerControl(check.conv.singular = .makeCC(action = "ignore", tol = 1e-4)))

drop1(emotion.mod4, test = "Chisq", ddf = "lme4", scope = . ~ .,)

Presentation Order Effects

To determine whether the presentation order of the factors influenced children’s responses, we will conduct our confirmatory analysis with outcome-type order (positive outcome first vs. second) and relationship-type order (friends first vs. second) included as dummy-coded, mean-centered fixed effects.

emotion.mod5 = lmer(emotion.score ~ relationship.type * outcome.type + first.outcome + first.relationship + first.context + (1|sub.num), 
                    data = model.data,
                    control = lmerControl(check.conv.singular = .makeCC(action = "ignore", tol = 1e-4)))

drop1(emotion.mod5, test = "Chisq", ddf = "lme4", scope = . ~ .,)
data %>%
  group_by(first.outcome) %>%
  dplyr::select(emotion.score) %>%
  get_summary_stats(type = "mean_sd")
## Adding missing grouping variables: `first.outcome`

Separate Happy and Sad Ratings

model.data.1 = model.data %>% 
  mutate(sad = sad * -1) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = happy:sad,
               names_to = "emotion.type",
               values_to = "response") %>%
  mutate(emotion.type = ifelse(emotion.type == "happy", 1, -1))

emotion.mod7 = lm(response ~ relationship.type * outcome.type * emotion.type * age.years, data = model.data.1) 

drop1(emotion.mod7, test = "F", ddf = "lme4", scope = . ~ .,)

Post-Hoc Comparisons

emmeans(emotion.mod7, ~ relationship.type | outcome.type * emotion.type) %>% pairs(infer=c(TRUE,TRUE), adjust = "Bonferroni")

figures2 = data %>%
  mutate(etoms.empathy = etoms.empathy - mean(etoms.empathy, na.rm = T),
         etoms.nice.tom = etoms.nice.tom - mean(etoms.nice.tom, na.rm = T),
         etoms.nasty.tom = etoms.nasty.tom - mean(etoms.nasty.tom, na.rm = T),
         relationship.type = ifelse(relationship.type == "friends", "Friends", "Rivals")) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = etoms.empathy:etoms.nasty.tom,
               names_to = "scale",
               values_to = "etoms.response") %>%
  mutate(scale = factor(scale, levels = c("etoms.empathy", "etoms.nice.tom", "etoms.nasty.tom"),
                        labels = c("Empathy", "Nice ToM", "Nasty ToM")),
         outcome.type = factor(outcome.type, labels = c("Negative Outcome", "Positive Outcome"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = etoms.response,

             color = outcome.type,
